en: Deliver them and save them.
This is the secret we have told;
It is no lie, but our truth.
Sarybai has brought us suffering;
It is no lie, but our truth.
I have whetted my black tongue,
Told every secret to the end,
And poured out my song, your dear Choro.”
When Kuyaly heard this,
Her thirst for blood seized her.
“Father, my brother-in-law Külchoro,
My dwelling place is Jelpiniş,
The white tulpar is the steed I ride,
And Sarybai is the one I shall fight;
This is how the quarrel stands.
In those dark and distant days,
When your dear sister-in-law was still a maiden,
I understood what you would need.
To your heroic uncle
I became a bride pledged until Judgment Day,
And for a long time shared his life.
I knew of this deed
Of our vengeful enemy Sarybai.
That madman, the ogre’s son,
Has passed the tale down from teller to teller;
He asked for the giant beauty, daughter of Kaiypchal,
At the urging of a mischief-maker.
Winter vanished from its season;
Because of wretched me,
Those two madmen schemed
To cast the nation into turmoil
And carry me away,
Bringing conflict upon my people,
Pouring suffering upon my people,
Starting rebellion among my people,
And spreading turmoil through my land.
At the great funeral feast for my khan father,
He began the fighting at its outset,
Driving my people frantic
And many times disturbing my heart.
He ruined my funeral feast,
And left my head ringing.
He sent a matchmaker between us,
But God took that vile man.
He sent an envoy from his people,
But God took him from the earth.
They drew their bows like pouring rain
And fired arrows like hail;
When he unleashed his violent fury,
He stood and waged battle.
Destroying the people and slaughtering the nation,
They fought in bitter conflict;
There was a clamor of battle cries,
A mighty tumult of warfare.
My dear hair, long as meadow grass,
I wound and knotted atop my head,
And donned armor no bullet could pierce.
This infidel Sarybai—
I drove him headlong from Jelpiniş.
Never letting his tail touch the ground,
Never letting him walk upon the earth,
I raised a clamor that split the sky.
Unable to lodge for even two nights,
Unable to find room upon the earth,
I thrashed him like crushed grain.
I drove him out of Jelpiniş
And bound his hands without rope.
He fought in earnest, burning with rage,
Despairing of his fly-like life;
His world closed in around him,
And his valor became known.
Against this infidel Sarybai,
This is the arm that shall wrestle,
This is the foe that shall trade shots with him.”
Maiden Kuyaly said these words,
And spoke many wondrous things;
She took up her spear called Muragy,
Girded on her scabbardless sword,
And donned armor no bullet could pierce;
Her heroism became apparent.
She performed deeds of many kinds
And made ready at the word “foe.”
Wisdom came to her from the unseen,
And she set her face toward Sarybai;
This is how the matter unfolded.
Across forked ridges and steep passes,
He led a seething predatory host;
The earth grew misty and eyes flashed—
Such was the ogre’s way.
Raging and straining,
He sheathed his arms in steel.
His eyes blazed like light;
Sarybai was the one she would grapple,
Such was the enemy she would fight.
That infidel Sarybai,
That warrior who destroyed nations,
Was filled with wrath and mighty venom,
Plotting cruel calamity,
And sparing no life in battle.
Destroying nations and drinking blood,
He drew deeply on his mighty strength;
Hardened by constant fighting,
He shed and drank blood in abundance
And became renowned as a bloodthirsty killer.
His valor was well known;
So terrible was his fury
That he proclaimed it to the whole world,
Raising shrill cries and clamor,
Raising a din that split the sky,
Menacing and frantic,
Possessed as though rabid.
His drums boomed and thundered,
Crashing like lightning,
While he roared in anger.
Every person who saw him
Shuddered through his entire body.
Shrill cries and urging shouts,
Motley banners and uproar—
He set the face of the earth ablaze,
As though he alone would encamp upon the heights.
The eighteen thousand worlds
He gulped at like a dragon,
As though that swine would swallow them now.
Upon the rugged hills and passes,
He seemed a giant black bird alighting;
Gulping like a dragon,
He seemed to swallow the whole world.
Most formidable, mighty in venom,
He leveled everyone he encountered;
If you met and faced him,
You abandoned hope of life, saying, “We are lost.”
A matchless champion, enormous in stature—
No giant like him exists in the world.
If you meet him head-on, take him from the flank;
He broke through herds and opened roads,
And attacked everyone he encountered.
Destroying nations and slaughtering peoples,
He hardened himself by wading through blood,
And among all the teeming peoples
Became renowned as a great calamity.
The knobs upon his two shoulders,
With two humps rising on each,
Seemed to have fed countless infidels
In the flames of his two cheeks.
Of the men who went to face him,
He seemed able to swallow countless numbers.
His eyes were like open pits;
The vastness of his nose
Was like the flank of a shattered mountain.
Could any creature be born like this?
When he attacked, would he spare a life?
His name was heard throughout the world;
Across the eighteen thousand worlds,
He had indeed raised an uproar.
His extraordinary form was unlike all others;
Among the whole wide world,
He had been born uniquely marked.
His war cry became a bullet,
And wherever that doomed man faced,
A red flame rose waist-high.
His form was strange, his nature cruel;
Such wrath, it seems, is never born.
He thirstily swallowed the Black Khan,
Who had committed no crime and bore no feud,
Who had done not the slightest wrong,
Yet he began a grievous conflict.
Your dear people of forty forefathers—
Against them he began a grievous conflict.
The field filled with black battle standards,
The people were shattered in an uproar,
And he began a violent war.
Regarding the Kyrgyz as less than a hair,
He slaughtered them without a backward glance.
From Sarybai’s venom,
From the visible fury of hell,
The peaceful people who had lived in joy
He slaughtered and plunged into misery.
The vigorous, swift and peerless hero
Was brought down by the swine Sarybai.
Fierce in menace and bitter in venom,
He had nations of enemies he had fought;
No such being can come from humankind.
No falcon had struck the wild swan,
Yet not one swan remained whole.
None whom the madman’s hand had touched
Remained unharmed among the people.
Some upon the borders fled aside;
He burned many lands.
He poured blood into the black waters,
Planted his banner on the grassy ground,
And began strife among kindred peoples.
He devoured everyone he encountered,
Destroying the entire nation;
All who had committed no crime,
The young and the old alike—
He extinguished their burning hearths
And drove every living soul away.
Many dear souls perished.
Lions who defended their people came forth,
And warriors from many nations came forth;
Many people beheld
The true land from which none returns.
The people were shattered and the nation cried out;
He began a violent conflict.
Their whole population was slaughtered;
Saying, “We shall all perish together,
For Sarybai has encountered us
And utterly sucked us dry,”
The people summoned their courage.
Anyone who resisted him,
Sarybai left none alive,
But severed their heads like sheep.
He split their bellies like melons;
Destroying the people and slaughtering the nation,
He brought such catastrophe upon them.
Because of the calamity that had passed,
Because of this swine,
They scattered all they had gathered
And fled, stripped of fortune.
Leaving not a single group behind,
They departed in one desperate flight
Toward the defile of Jan-Baspas.
In the desert of Jangeldik,
Of all who openly came before him,
He slew a multitude.
Anyone who displeased him,
He beheaded with his sword.
Countless guiltless souls
He gave over to massacre.
Wailing and weeping bitterly,
Lamenting and crying aloud,
Truly burning with grief,
Despairing of their fly-like lives,
The people lost their senses,
Moaning as if about to die,
Because of Sarybai’s venom,
Because of the infidel who had turned depraved,
The enemy who faced them,
They routed with heroic might,
At the sight, the mind reeled,
They loomed like lofty blue mountains,
Their movement seemed an army of forty thousand,
Crouching like lions,
Wherever they surged past,
No mountain could withstand them.
Like a flood that shattered mountains,
Like innumerable hosts engulfing the land,
Though all the world’s peoples attacked,
The great khan’s descendants
Could not be bent or conquered for an age.
The reason they could not prevail:
Before them strode a gray tiger,
A lion like the magnanimous hero,
Throwing the mighty into confusion,
Making the dun horse beneath him
Stride proudly onward.
